newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin on world stage after illness meets Chirac.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin on world stage after illness meets Chirac.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin took to the world stage on Sunday for the first time since falling ill with pneumonia when he met French President Jacques Chirac for talks expected to focus on NATO expansion.

Yeltsin, dressed in a heavy black coat and fur hat, greeted Chirac on the forecourt of the snow-covered Novo-Ogaryova residence outside the capital after waiting for about a minute in temperatures of minus 18 degrees Celsius (minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit).

The Russian president, released from hospital on January 20, smiled and looked in good humour but walked stiffly as he accompanied Chirac into the house. Chirac brought him a parcel tied with a white ribbon for his 66th birthday on Saturday.
"We are not only two European leaders but two friends," Yeltsin said. "It is unfortunate that you cannot stay longer but we will talk about the essential issues."

French television was allowed to film the initial greeting but barred from the meeting room. Opponents charge that Yeltsin, who had heart surgery in November, is too ill to rule. The Chirac meeting is Yeltsin's first chance to demonstrate he has a hand on foreign affairs and authority abroad.
Yeltsin's few appearances on television since his release from hospital have shown him looking aged and rather frail.

The Russian president spent his birthday quietly with his family. He was joined in the evening by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, just back from an economic summit in Switzerland, and chief aide Anatoly Chubais.
Yeltsin's wife, Naina, said the president was recovering well.

"Doctors say that if it were just a normal man he should have stayed in hospital...It takes longer to recover if you work at the same time." His condition, she said, allowed him more time to watch television and to think.
"Now he has more time to...weigh things," she said in a television interview. His daughter, Tatyana, said the family had bought the president a quilted jacket as a present.
Chirac, along with other Western leaders, sees Yeltsin's survival as essential to economic reform in Russia.
The talks were to centre on NATO's plans to begin talks later this year to incorporate some of Moscow's former Warsaw Pact allies, including Poland. Russia sees in this a threat to its security.

Since NATO made clear that Russia's objections would not stop its expansion, Moscow appears to have switched to negotiating a deal which would keep the alliance's military structures away from its borders.
Government officials say Russia is seeking a binding document rather than a political declaration.
They say that in an ideal world this document should include a promise not to deploy nuclear forces, heavy weapons and troops belonging to other NATO states on the territory of new members.
Moscow is clearly looking for support from within NATO, especially from some of its European members who seek to take over some alliance command functions from the United States.
Government officials have said that Moscow closely watched debates between Washington and Paris about whether an American or European should command NATO's southern flank.

A French official has said that Paris supported Moscow's demands for a binding charter on Russia-NATO relations and felt the United States was still trying to fob off the Russians with a few non-binding pledges.
Washington and most NATO allies oppose a legally binding accord requiring parliamentary ratification.
Chirac hopes NATO can work out a deal with Russia before an alliance summit in Madrid in July at which it is expected to issue invitations to some eastern European states.
